## What it is

**Listens to a CAN bus (vehicles, tractors, boats, generators, battery systems) and publishes decoded signals on NATS.** CAN is a broadcast bus: every controller sends short *frames* (an id and up to 8 data bytes), and anyone on the bus can listen. A signal such as engine speed is a few bytes at a known position in the frame with a known id. This app keeps the latest frame of each id and decodes the signals you list.

It is one of four field protocol adapters (FLD-03, #201) that share one design, described in full in the [Modbus adapter's README](../modbus-adapter/README.md): poll each point, publish good values on `tel.<node>-<device>.<class>.<metric>`, show the latest values on a read-only status page on port 8080.

**Why socketcand and not the CAN interface directly.** Linux talks to CAN hardware through SocketCAN: an interface such as `can0` in the host's network namespace. An app pod has its own namespace and may not use the host network or host devices (the app gate refuses `hostNetwork`, `hostPath` and privileged containers, and that is the right rule). So the adapter reaches the bus over TCP through [socketcand](https://github.com/linux-can/socketcand), the Linux-CAN project's CAN-over-TCP server, which runs next to the CAN interface: on the host, or on a small CAN gateway box. It speaks socketcand's documented raw mode (doc/protocol.md: `< hi >`, `< open can0 >`, `< rawmode >`, then `< frame ID SECONDS.USECONDS DATA >`).

**Observe-first: it only listens.** Listening never changes a CAN bus. The adapter never sends socketcand's `< send ... >` command (there is no code for it), and `write()` always raises "writes are refused". A write must become an owner-approved gateway action (`cmd.*`, published only by the gateway, D-B9); that path is not built yet.

**Licence:** Apache-2.0, OneMind's own code ([`manifests/can_adapter.py`](manifests/can_adapter.py) and the shared [`manifests/fieldbus.py`](manifests/fieldbus.py)), written from socketcand's protocol description; no third-party code (python-can, LGPL-3.0, is not used). socketcand itself is a separate program the owner runs next to the bus; it is not shipped here.

## How it runs here

- One stateless `Deployment` on the official python 3.14 slim image, code from a ConfigMap, `python3 -I -B` as `nobody`, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no host network, no devices.
- Settings: `can_host`, `can_port` (29536, socketcand's default), `can_bus` (`can0`), and the shared `points`, `node`, `device`, `poll_seconds`, `nats_url`.
- `points` is a comma-separated list of `class.metric=HEXID:BYTE[:TYPE][*SCALE]`: the frame id in hex, the first byte of the signal (0-7), and the type `u8` (default), `i8`, `u16`, `i16`, `u32`, `i32` or `f32`, little-endian (add `be` for big-endian, e.g. `u16be`). Example: `engine.rpm=0CF00400:3:u16*0.125`.
- A signal whose frame has not been seen for 30 s shows `quality: bad` ("no frame with id ...") and is not published.
- Tests: `python3 -I -m unittest discover -s test/unit -p test_field_adapters.py -v` runs it against an in-process socketcand simulator and checks that the adapter sends only `open` and `rawmode`.

## Not done yet

- **socketcand must run somewhere the box can reach.** On a OneMind box that would be the host; packaging socketcand into the OS image or as a host service is a separate OS decision, not made here.
- **On a OneMind box, the per-app network policy (H-04) blocks the adapter from reaching LAN or host addresses and NATS**, and NATS credentials are not supported. Same gap and same proposed follow-up as the [Modbus adapter](../modbus-adapter/README.md#not-done-yet).
- Signals that are not whole bytes (bit fields), DBC file import, J1939 multi-frame messages, CAN FD frames, writes.
- Not yet tested against a physical bus with socketcand; the simulator follows doc/protocol.md.
